intro.html: Rules can be held tight or let loose. The first five words describe strictness, from the careful thoroughness of rigorous work to the cruel harshness of draconian laws. The next four describe going easy, from the mercy of a lenient judge to the carelessness of a lax guard. The last, forbearance, names the patience it takes to hold back.
Notice the tone. Rigorous and exacting usually praise; draconian always criticizes. Lenient can be kind; lax is a complaint.

words.def: strict and exact about rules or standards
words.ex: The pool has {stringent} rules: no running, no glass and no swimming without a lifeguard.
words.ctx: The lab’s safety rules are {stringent}; a student who forgets goggles even once is sent out for the day.
words.etym: From Latin stringens, “drawing tight,” from stringere, “to bind tight.”

mn.text: Coach Ada keeps her team rules pulled as tight as a string: no slack, no exceptions. Rules that tight are {stringent}.

scene.alt: A coach pulls a rope tight beside a sign that says team rules.

words.ex: After a {rigorous} search of the house, Mom found the missing key inside the cereal box.
words.ctx: The bridge opened only after {rigorous} testing: loaded trucks rolled across it for a week, and engineers checked every bolt and every weld twice.
words.etym: From Latin rigor, “stiffness, hardness,” from rigere (to be stiff).

mn.cue: check the RIG, ALL of US
mn.text: Before the sailboat race, all of us check every rope and knot of the rig, then check them again. An inspection that careful is {rigorous}.

scene.alt: Three teens inspect a sailboat with a magnifying glass, a checklist and a rope before a race.

words.def: demanding great effort, care or skill
words.ex: The {exacting} piano teacher made Rosa play the hard measure twenty times.
words.ctx: Repairing old clocks is {exacting} work: a single bent spring or a speck of dust can stop the whole movement.
words.etym: From the verb exact, “to demand,” from Latin exigere, “to drive out, demand”: ex (out) + agere (to drive).

mn.text: Chef Lin makes her new cook measure the sugar again and again until it is exact. A boss who demands that much care is {exacting}.

scene.alt: A chef points sternly while a nervous young cook measures sugar with a spoon beside a set of scales.

words.ex: One {stern} look from the librarian quieted the whole table.
words.ctx: Grandpa’s voice was {stern} when he found the open gate, but he was not cruel; he simply explained why the sheep must never be left loose again.
words.note: A different word, the noun stern, is the back end of a ship.

mn.text: Principal Victor gives the noisy hallway one long stare, and everyone falls silent. A serious, strict look like that is {stern}.

scene.alt: A principal with crossed arms stares at two quiet, worried children.

words.ex: Taking away recess for a whole month for one late homework is {draconian}.
words.ctx: Under the old king’s {draconian} laws, stealing a single loaf of bread could cost a family its home, so the new queen’s first act was to soften them.
words.etym: Named for Draco, a lawmaker of ancient Athens whose laws punished even small crimes with great severity.

mn.text: In the dragon’s castle the rule is: take one cookie and get no dessert for a whole year. Rules that harsh are {draconian}.

props.text: 1 COOKIE = NO DESSERT FOR A YEAR

scene.alt: A grumpy dragon stands under a banner with a very harsh rule while a boy holding one cookie looks shocked.

words.def: merciful; less strict or harsh than expected
words.ex: The {lenient} referee let the little kids redo their throw-ins.
words.ctx: Most judges would have fined the young driver heavily, but this one was {lenient}: she let him off with a warning and a safety class.
words.etym: From Latin leniens, “softening,” from lenire, “to soften, soothe,” from lenis (soft, mild).

mn.cue: LEAN-IENT: the judge LEANS toward mercy
mn.text: The judge leans down, smiles at the nervous boy who broke a window, and says, “Just fix it and say sorry.” She is {lenient}.

scene.alt: A smiling judge goes easy on a nervous boy.

words.def: quick to give others what they want; not strict
words.ex: The {indulgent} aunt let the twins eat birthday cake for breakfast.
words.ctx: Their grandparents were so {indulgent} that the children came home from every visit expecting dessert before dinner and a bedtime of midnight.
words.etym: From Latin indulgere, “to be kind to, give way to.”

mn.cue: IN-DULGE: Granny says yes to everything
mn.text: Granny Mae indulges every wish: cake for breakfast, a pony ride, staying up late. A granny who gives the kids whatever they want is {indulgent}.

scene.alt: A smiling grandmother hands a cake to two cheering children.

words.def: allowing a great deal of freedom
words.ex: The camp had a {permissive} bedtime: campers could stay up as long as they were quiet.
words.ctx: The new school was far more {permissive} than her old one; students chose their own seats, ate snacks in class and could leave the room without asking.
words.etym: From permit, from Latin permittere, “to let pass, allow”: per (through) + mittere (to let go).

mn.text: At Uncle Omar’s house you have permission for everything: pillow fights, pancakes at midnight, a fort in the living room. His house is {permissive}.

scene.alt: A relaxed uncle shrugs and smiles while children have a pillow fight in the living room.

words.def: not strict or careful enough; loose
words.ex: Security at the cookie jar was {lax}, and the dog took full advantage.
words.ctx: The inspector blamed the leak on {lax} maintenance: no one had checked the pipes in years, and the warning light had been ignored for months.
words.etym: From Latin laxus, “loose, slack,” the same root as relax.

mn.cue: reLAXed: too relaxed to do the job
mn.text: The guard is so relaxed that he naps in his chair while the dog helps himself to the cookies. That careless guard is {lax}.

scene.alt: A guard naps in his chair while a dog sneaks toward a cookie jar under a no dogs sign.

words.def: patient self-control; holding back from anger or punishment
words.ex: The babysitter showed great {forbearance} when the twins painted the kitchen door blue.
words.ctx: The lender could have taken the farm after the bad harvest, but he showed {forbearance}, giving the family another year to pay.

mn.text: The cubs tug the big bear’s ears and climb on his back, but he never growls; he just waits. That patient holding back is {forbearance}.

scene.alt: A big calm bear lets two playful cubs climb on him and tug at him.

after.cap: Choose the word whose tone fits the writer’s view.

after.html: Lax describes rules or care that are too loose (lax security). Lenient describes a person who goes easy on someone (a lenient judge). A judge can be lenient; a lock can only be lax.

items.q: A reporter who calls a new rule draconian thinks the rule is…
items.why: Draconian always criticizes: it means excessively harsh. Rigorous is the word that praises thoroughness.

choices: Because the museum’s security was lax, no one noticed the open window for a week.
The lax judge sentenced the thief to ten years in prison.
Her lax training made her the fastest runner in the state.
The lax rules were enforced with great care.
items.why: Lax means loose and careless. Security that misses an open window for a week is lax.

items.q: The scientist’s method was rigorous. This is most likely…
choices: a hint that she was careless
items.why: Rigorous praises work that is careful and thorough.

items.q: True or false: a teacher who patiently holds back from scolding a class shows forbearance.
items.why: True. Forbearance is patient self-control: holding back from anger or punishment.
